group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 79-year-old man was brought to the emergency department by his daughter after becoming progressively febrile and short of breath over the preceding forty-eight hours, culminating this morning in an episode of near-syncope while shuffling from the bedroom to the bathroom. He lives independently in a single-story bungalow, performs most activities of daily living unaided, and relies on his daughter only for transportation to and from the dialysis center, where he undergoes thrice-weekly treatments for long-standing diabetic-ischemic kidney failure; his last run was two days ago, and according to the dialysis record he completed the session without complications. In addition to the renal issue, he carries a diagnosis of reduced-ejection-fraction cardiomyopathy attributed to remote anterior-wall infarction, for which he takes carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan at a modest dose, and low-dose furosemide on nondialysis days. He denies any prior cerebrovascular accidents and has never been told he has cirrhosis or hepatitis. There is no history of malignancy, and he has not required hospitalization in the past year. He stopped smoking three decades ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks half a glass of wine on holidays, and has never used illicit substances. Two influenza seasons ago he received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine at his primary-care clinic; this year’s influenza shot was administered at the dialysis unit in October. At home he recorded an oral temperature of 102 °F last evening and noted chills severe enough to shake the bed, but took no antipyretics because he feared masking symptoms. Overnight he slept upright in a recliner, waking repeatedly to cough up rust-colored sputum and complaining of a sharp ache along the right lateral chest wall with each breath. He used the home pulse-oximeter kept for dialysis days and saw readings drifting into the low 80s on room air, prompting the family to call emergency services. Paramedics found him seated, tachypneic, and clammy but answering questions appropriately; they deliberately withheld oxygen, fluids, or medications so that emergency-department personnel could obtain unaltered baseline measurements. On arrival to triage—prior to any intervention—his vital signs were: oral temperature 102.8 °F (39.3 °C), heart rate 130 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 87/54 mm Hg in both arms by manual sphygmomanometer, respiratory rate 47 breaths per minute with pronounced intercostal retractions, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 79 % and 81 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude. His skin was warm and moderately diaphoretic; mucous membranes appeared tacky. Jugular venous pulsation rose approximately 7 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, consistent with prior cardiology examinations. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid S1 and S2 with a faint third sound but no new murmurs. Lung examination disclosed absent breath sounds with stony dullness to percussion over the lower two-thirds of the right posterior thorax, while coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds were appreciated just above that level; the left lung transmitted scattered late inspiratory crackles at the base but remained largely resonant. The abdomen was soft and nontender with a hemodialysis graft palpable in the left forearm; no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites were detected. Neurologically he was alert, oriented to person, place, date, and recent events, followed commands briskly, and exhibited no focal deficits. A bedside capillary glucose measured 165 mg/dL. Venous blood and an arterial sample from the right radial artery were drawn within ten minutes of arrival before any intravenous flushes other than small heparin locks were applied. Chemistries returned sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 4.9 mEq/L, chloride 93 mEq/L, bicarbonate 17 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 52 mg/dL, and an anticipated creatinine elevation of 4.8 mg/dL, comparable to his anuric baseline. Complete blood count showed a hematocrit of 59 % with hemoglobin 19.2 g/dL, leukocytosis of 17.6 × 10⁹/L (89 % neutrophils), and platelets 235 × 10⁹/L. The arterial blood gas obtained while he continued to breathe room air revealed pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg, PaO₂ 48 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, indicating a primary metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation and severe hypoxemia. Serum lactate was mildly elevated at 3.1 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph performed before any therapy demonstrated a dense consolidation filling the right lower lobe with a concave upper border, accompanied by a fluid column layering to the level of the fourth posterior rib and blunting of the right costophrenic angle, while the cardiac silhouette appeared mildly enlarged in keeping with known ventricular dysfunction. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 128 bpm with nonspecific ST-segment flattening unchanged from a tracing six months earlier. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Legionella and pneumococcus, and a respiratory viral PCR panel were obtained before antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors, supplemental oxygen, antipyretics, or dialysis maneuvers were initiated, preserving the aforementioned physiologic and laboratory data as the patient’s untreated presentation profile.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points using pretreatment findings.
- Demographics: a man's baseline score is his age in years = 79. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0. Subtotal = 79.
- Comorbidities: systolic heart failure = 10; chronic renal disease on dialysis = 10. No malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease = 0 each. Subtotal = 20.
- Examination: RR 47/min (≥30) = 20; systolic BP 87 mmHg (<90) = 20; pulse 130/min (≥125) = 10. He is alert = 0; temperature 39.3°C is neither <35°C nor ≥40°C = 0. Subtotal = 50.
- Labs: arterial pH 7.24 (<7.35) = 30; BUN 52 mg/dL (≥30) = 20; sodium 118 mEq/L (<130) = 20. Glucose 165 mg/dL (<250) = 0; hematocrit 59% (not <30%) = 0. Room-air PaO₂ 48 mmHg (<60) = 10; low SpO₂ does not score separately. Subtotal = 80.
- Imaging: right pleural effusion = 10.
Total = 79 + 20 + 50 + 80 + 10 = 239.
Final answer: 239
